content.text: Three-player trick-taking Tarot recorded by the Abbé de Marolles in 1637 at Nevers. Played with a 66-card pack (Italian-suited Tarot with lowest three of each suit removed). Players score for declaring card combinations, for winning or losing Tarots (Kings, Fool, Trump I, XXI), for card points in tricks, and for Ultimo (last trick with King or Trump I).

Michel de Marolles, Abbot of Villeloin, recorded in 1637 that he played Tarot at Nevers with Princess Louise-Marie de Gonzague-Nevers (later Queen of Poland). She had added innovations and asked him to have the rules printed; these are the oldest known printed Tarot rules.
Three players, each playing for themselves; no partnerships.

66-card pack: Italian-suited Tarot (78 cards) with the lowest three cards of each suit removed. 22 triomphes (21 trumps I–XXI plus the Fool); 4 suits with 4 court cards (King, Queen, Cavalier, Jack) and 7 numerals each.

Dealer shuffles; player to dealer's left cuts (cut card shown; if it is a Tarot, dealer receives one marque from each opponent). Dealer deals 4 rounds of 5 cards to each player, then one more card to each other player and 4 to himself: non-dealers receive 21 cards each, dealer 24. The two non-dealers each discard one card and the dealer discards four; no trumps or Tarots may be discarded (penalty: two marques to each opponent). Discards count in the discarder's favour at end of play.

items.text: 78-card game: Without the Princess's innovations: full 78-card pack; 25 cards each to dealer's opponents, 28 to dealer who discards 3; no discard by non-dealers. Similar to classic 3-player Tarot in 18th-century Europe.
